name: Gullstitch Sail Loft
description: A long narrow three-storey sailmaker/netmaker building, about six metres frontage and nine metres deep, between the harbour lane and a small service passage. Ochre-grey limestone ground storey with wide blue-green arched plank loading doors and a pedestrian wicket. Two jettied upper storeys of warm honey timber and pale sea-salt plaster; rust-red clay tiled long gable roof with a small ventilating ridge cupola and one squat masonry chimney. A deep central sail-loft loading opening extends across the top two floors under the FRONT gable, with solid closed/open paired timber shutters and a short useful oak hoist beam under the roof. The rope runs over a visible pulley and down to a folded sail bundle; every part is mechanically attached, no massive floating crane. An identifiable narrow net-drying gallery runs down the RIGHT long side at first-floor level, its lean roof and railing supported by timber posts; several large repaired fishing nets hang in tidy curtains, not web-like clutter. Rear gable has simple regular workshop windows and an oak service door; below, an open-sided sheltered mending bench, net floats and two spool-shaped rope reels occupy the rear end of the same gallery. Weathered pale-blue shutters, a plain pictorial needle-and-sail hanging emblem, plants in one terracotta pot and inhabited attic curtains. Make the long working elevation and useful hoist the distinctive features; this is a busy town craft house, not a ruined warehouse, pirate ship or isolated fisherman cottage.

It must be a specific believable town building, not a generic house and not a fantasy castle.
Input image 1: approved Guildhall Square STYLE/MATERIAL/CITY-DENSITY reference only. Input image 2: approved workshop lane OUTLINE/CRAFT/COASTAL-TOWN reference only. Do not copy either scene, beacon, guild hall, workshop or composition.
CAMERA AND LAYOUT: left panel shows FRONT plus RIGHT side, looking diagonally from the southeast. Right panel shows the BACK plus LEFT side, exactly 180 degrees around the same building. In both use orthographic parallel projection, 45-degree azimuth to the walls and about 31 degrees downward elevation from horizontal, the fixed game view. Vertical lines remain parallel; no lens/perspective convergence or distorted axes. Both views must show the same entire roof and all walls down to the foundations, no cutaways, with equal scale and lighting. Arrange generous blank space between the two silhouettes and at least 7 percent clear margins at every sheet edge. Neither roof, finial, chimney, hoist, window box, base nor rear accessory may be clipped.
STYLE: finely outlined warm painted 3D concept art like the supplied town. Strong readable roof/body forms, warm dark-brown contour lines, rich painterly material detail without noisy photorealism. Cream dressed limestone, weathered plaster, honey oak joinery, iron fittings, hand-laid roof tiles, modest brass/copper mechanisms and warm amber lamps. A cared-for, lived-in seaside trades town: salt wear low on masonry, patched shutters, practical gutters, believable doors/windows and occupied upper floors. The building could stand close to neighbouring buildings in a medium-sized dense town. Do not surround it with a floating cliff, sea diorama or a whole street. A thin restrained paving/foundation footprint below each building is enough.
CONTINUITY: exactly the same footprint, storey heights, roof ridge/gables, chimney positions, rear extension, wall openings and materials across the two views, rotated not mirrored or redesigned. Distinct front and back: shop front faces the street; deliveries, gutters and useful service details are at the rear. Supported balconies, roof loads and physically attached pipes/hoists. Keep decor subordinate to architecture. No people, robots, labels, lettering, dimension arrows, grid, title, watermark or modern cars. Signs may contain a simple pictorial trade emblem only.
